metadata.narrative: I am planning to implement a embedded system processor for a thermostat machine. Write me a blog post which goes through everything that I need to consider, including things like RISC vs. CISC instruction set, how I can actually code and test this processor using open-source technologies like Linux and more.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Building an embedded processor for a thermostat forces a stack of interlocking decisions, starting with the instruction set architecture and ending with how you prove the system works before it ships.
The first fork is the classic RISC versus CISC question, and for a small embedded controller the answer is almost always RISC.
RISC designs use simple, fixed-size instructions that decode quickly, pipeline well, draw less power, and require a smaller die, matching a thermostat's cost and power budget.

CISC chips pack more work into each instruction and need less code and RAM, but burn more power and need a larger, costlier chip, making them better suited to data-heavy workloads than a wall-mounted controller.

Once RISC is chosen, the open-source RISC-V instruction set is worth serious consideration because it is published under a permissive BSD-style license, requires no royalty payments, and lets you implement only the extensions your thermostat actually needs.

RISC-V began as a UC Berkeley project in 2010, is now governed by RISC-V International, and its ecosystem already includes FPGA soft cores from vendors like SiFive, boards such as the HiFive1, and Linux ports through Yocto and Debian.

Compared with ARM's Cortex-M, which dominates embedded designs with a mature commercial ecosystem, RISC-V trades some vendor support for freedom from license fees, and for a hobby or startup thermostat that openness can matter more than polish.

A related decision is whether to implement the processor as an FPGA "soft core" or eventually as a fabricated "hard core," and the tradeoffs are stark: hard cores run far faster and more efficiently, while soft cores are easier to modify but capped near 200 to 250 MHz and draw more power per operation.

A thermostat does not need general-purpose horsepower, so a compact custom soft core built around your specific sensor and actuator interfaces can be smaller and simpler to program than a generic microcontroller core dropped onto an FPGA.

Whichever core you pick, the control problem itself is a closed-loop regulation task: an ADC samples a sensor such as an LM35, firmware computes a duty cycle from the reading relative to a setpoint and bandwidth, and a PWM output drives the heater, shrinking ON time as temperature rises above target and growing it as temperature falls below target.

Because a thermostat is power-conscious, plan around standard microcontroller power states: idle mode gates the CPU clock while keeping the oscillator running for fast wake-up, standby keeps high-speed peripherals like the ADC alive, and deep-sleep disables nearly everything except a watchdog to reach microamp-level consumption.
Writing power-conscious C code that favors local variables and bitmasks over heavier constructs further reduces energy draw without any hardware change.

If you are designing custom digital logic rather than buying a packaged chip, the open-source RTL-to-silicon flow starts with Yosys for logic synthesis, converting Verilog into a gate-level netlist, then proceeds through floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, and routing inside OpenROAD to produce a manufacturable GDSII layout.

For pure simulation before touching fabrication or even an FPGA, Icarus Verilog offers a simple but slow event-driven simulator, while Verilator compiles synthesizable RTL into C++ for cycle-based simulation that can be hundreds of times faster, and Yosys's newer CXXRTL backend trades some speed for easier extensibility.

Once RTL works, or if targeting a commercial core instead, you need a software toolchain: GNU Binutils for assembling and linking, GCC for compiling, a lightweight C library such as uClibc or musl, and GDB as cross-debugger, bundled as a cross-compilation toolchain running on your desktop but generating target code.

If the core is ARM-based, the GNU ARM Embedded Toolchain packages exactly this stack, GCC, GDB, Binutils, and Newlib, tuned for Cortex-M and Cortex-R parts, letting you compile, flash, and remotely debug over GDBServer and JTAG entirely with open tools.

For the operating system layer, most thermostats do not need full Linux, and this is where an RTOS fits: FreeRTOS is a small, MIT-licensed scheduler with task priorities, semaphores, and queues, easy to learn and running on over forty architectures including the ESP32 and STM32.

Zephyr, backed by the Linux Foundation, suits a battery-powered thermostat well since its tickless, event-driven kernel targets energy efficiency and ships developer features like a GDB Stub for remote debugging and devicetree-based hardware configuration.

If the thermostat instead warrants full embedded Linux, for example to run networking or a local web UI, Buildroot gives a fast, minimalist Makefile-based system that rebuilds from scratch on every change, while Yocto offers a larger, layer-based framework at the cost of a steeper learning curve and longer builds.

For testing without physical hardware, QEMU is the workhorse open-source emulator: it can boot a minimal Linux image built with Buildroot over a virtual architecture, transfer files via TFTP, and expose a GDB server for kernel-level breakpoints before any board exists.

QEMU also has purpose-built machine models for Cortex-M parts like the STM32F4-Discovery, letting you remotely debug your actual firmware with GDB, though its authors note timing and peripheral behavior are not fully hardware-accurate, so final validation on real silicon remains necessary.

Because a thermostat is a connected device, security testing belongs in the toolchain from the start, with roughly 75 billion connected embedded devices expected online by 2025 and over 2,000 embedded-specific vulnerabilities already catalogued in the National Vulnerability Database.

Concretely, static firmware analysis with open tools like Binwalk and Firmwalker can extract filesystems and hunt for hardcoded credentials, while dynamic analysis boots the same image inside QEMU for probing with tools like Nmap, closing the loop between emulation-based testing and security posture.

Baseline defenses worth budgeting for include secure boot verification, encrypted and authenticated firmware updates, and tamper-detection logic, since an unauthenticated update path is one of the most common ways connected products get compromised.

Put together, a practical path is to prototype control logic in QEMU or Verilator simulation, settle on a RISC-V or Cortex-M core running FreeRTOS or Zephyr for the control loop, add Buildroot-built Linux only if networking is required, and validate the final image with open-source static and dynamic security tooling before flashing real hardware.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Building an embedded processor for a thermostat forces you to make a stack of interlocking decisions, starting with the instruction set architecture and ending with how you will prove the whole system actually works before it ships.

The first fork in the road is the classic RISC versus CISC question, and for a small embedded controller the answer is almost always RISC.

RISC designs use simple, fixed-size instructions that decode quickly, pipeline well, draw less power, and require a smaller die, which is exactly what a thermostat's cost and battery budget demand.

CISC chips pack more work into each instruction and need less code and RAM per task, but they burn more power and need a larger, more expensive chip, so they are better suited to graphics or data-center workloads than to a wall-mounted climate controller.

Once you have settled on RISC, the open-source RISC-V instruction set is worth serious consideration because it is published under a permissive BSD-style license, requires no royalty payments, and lets you implement only the base integer instructions plus whatever extensions your thermostat actually needs.

RISC-V began as a UC Berkeley research project in 2010 and is now governed by RISC-V International, and its ecosystem already includes FPGA-ready soft cores from vendors like SiFive, development boards such as the HiFive1, and Linux ports through Yocto and Debian.

Compared with ARM's Cortex-M, which dominates the embedded market and offers a mature commercial ecosystem, RISC-V trades some of that vendor support for freedom from licensing fees and export-control ambiguity, and for a hobby or startup thermostat project that openness can matter more than polish.

A separate but related decision is whether you implement your processor as a "soft core" synthesized into FPGA logic or eventually push it to a "hard core" fabricated in silicon, and the tradeoffs are stark: hard cores run at hundreds of megahertz to multiple gigahertz with far better power efficiency, while soft cores are easier to modify and extend with custom instructions but are capped around 200 to 250 MHz and consume more power per operation because unused FPGA fabric still drains current.

For a thermostat, you do not need general-purpose computing horsepower, so a compact custom soft core built specifically around your sensor and actuator interfaces can be smaller and easier to program than a full off-the-shelf microcontroller core dropped onto an FPGA, and this is exactly the kind of minimal, purpose-built design that experienced FPGA developers describe building for single serial-interface tasks, sometimes drawing an analogy to the "minion core" or programmable real-time unit peripherals found on some commercial microcontrollers.

Whichever core you choose, the actual control problem a thermostat solves is a closed-loop temperature regulation task: an analog-to-digital converter samples a sensor such as an LM35, firmware computes a duty cycle from the sensor reading relative to a setpoint and bandwidth, and a pulse-width-modulated output drives the heating or cooling element, with the ON time shrinking as the sensed temperature rises above target and growing as it falls below target.

Because a thermostat is typically battery-backed or at least power-conscious, you should plan around the standard microcontroller power states: idle or sleep mode gates the CPU clock while keeping the main oscillator running for fast wake-up, standby mode also gates the CPU but keeps high-speed peripherals like ADC and DMA alive, and deep-sleep or stop modes disable almost everything except a watchdog and brown-out detector to get consumption down into the single-digit microamp range.

Dynamically scaling clock frequency between idle and active computation, and writing power-conscious C code that favors local variables, static const data, and bitmasks over heavier constructs, are additional firmware-level techniques that reduce energy draw without changing the hardware at all.

Turning to how you actually build and verify the processor, if you are designing custom digital logic rather than buying a packaged microcontroller, the open-source RTL-to-silicon flow starts with Yosys for logic synthesis, which converts your Verilog description into a gate-level netlist, and then proceeds through floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, and routing inside a tool such as OpenROAD to produce a manufacturable GDSII layout.

For pure simulation before you ever touch a fabrication process or even an FPGA, Icarus Verilog gives you a traditional event-driven simulator that is simple but slow, Verilator compiles synthesizable RTL into C++ for cycle-based simulation that can be hundreds of times faster, and the newer CXXRTL backend inside Yosys trades some raw speed for easier extensibility, flexible black-boxing of submodules, and built-in VCD waveform generation for debugging signal-level behavior.

Once you have working RTL, or if you are instead targeting a commercial microcontroller core, you need a software toolchain, and the open-source path runs through GNU Binutils for assembling and linking, GCC for compiling C and C++, a lightweight embedded C library choice such as uClibc or musl instead of full glibc, and GDB as the cross-debugger, all glued together as a cross-compilation toolchain that runs on your x86 development machine but generates code for your target architecture.

If your thermostat core is ARM-based, the GNU ARM Embedded Toolchain packages exactly this stack, GCC, GDB, Binutils, and the Newlib C library, specifically tuned for Cortex-M and Cortex-R parts, and it lets you compile, flash, and remotely debug firmware over GDBServer and JTAG entirely with open tools on Linux, Windows, or macOS.

For the operating system layer, most thermostats do not need a full Linux distribution, and this is where a real-time operating system fits: FreeRTOS is a small, MIT-licensed scheduler with task priorities, semaphores, and queues that is easy to learn and runs on more than forty architectures including popular boards like the ESP32 and STM32.

Zephyr, incubated by the Linux Foundation, is a strong alternative if your thermostat is battery-powered, since its tickless, event-driven kernel is built around energy efficiency, and it ships developer-friendly features like a GDB Stub for remote debugging and a devicetree-based hardware configuration system.

If you decide the thermostat instead warrants a full embedded Linux userspace, for example to run a network stack, a local web UI, or Python-based logic, Buildroot gives you a fast, minimalist Makefile-based system that regenerates a root filesystem image from scratch on every change, while Yocto offers a larger, more customizable, layer-based framework backed by the Linux Foundation at the cost of a steeper learning curve and longer build times.

For testing without physical hardware in hand, QEMU is the workhorse open-source emulator: it can boot a minimal Linux root filesystem and kernel built with Buildroot over a virtual architecture, transfer files via TFTP, and expose a GDB server so you can set breakpoints in kernel code before any board exists.

QEMU also has purpose-built machine models for Cortex-M parts like the STM32F4-Discovery or micro:bit, letting you run and remotely debug your actual firmware image with `-s -S` GDB flags, though QEMU's authors are candid that timing behavior, interrupt latency, and peripheral models are not fully hardware-accurate, so final validation on real silicon remains necessary.

Because a thermostat is a connected device, security testing belongs in your open-source toolchain from the start, and industry data suggests roughly 75 billion connected embedded devices will be online by 2025 with over 2,000 embedded-specific vulnerabilities already catalogued in the National Vulnerability Database.

Concretely, you can run static firmware analysis with open tools like Binwalk and Firmwalker to extract filesystems and hunt for hardcoded credentials or keys, then run dynamic analysis by booting the same firmware image inside QEMU and probing it with tools like Nmap or Metasploit, closing the loop between your emulation-based testing setup and your security posture.

Baseline defenses worth budgeting for include secure boot verification, encrypted and authenticated firmware update mechanisms, and tamper-detection logic, since an unauthenticated firmware update path is one of the most common ways connected embedded products get compromised.

Put together, a practical path for a hobbyist or small team is to prototype the control logic and peripheral interfacing entirely in QEMU or Verilator-based simulation, settle on a RISC-V or ARM Cortex-M core running FreeRTOS or Zephyr for the bare control loop, add Buildroot-built embedded Linux only if you need networking or a richer UI, and validate the final image with the same open-source static and dynamic security tooling before flashing real hardware.

If the thermostat instead warrants full embedded Linux, for example to run networking or a local web UI, Buildroot gives a fast, minimalist Makefile-based system that rebuilds from scratch on every change, while Yocto offers a larger, layer-based framework at the cost of a steeper learning curve and longer builds.

For testing without physical hardware, QEMU is the workhorse open-source emulator: it can boot a minimal Linux image built with Buildroot over a virtual architecture, transfer files via TFTP, and expose a GDB server for kernel-level breakpoints before any board exists.

QEMU also has purpose-built machine models for Cortex-M parts like the STM32F4-Discovery, letting you remotely debug your actual firmware with GDB, though its authors note timing and peripheral behavior are not fully hardware-accurate, so final validation on real silicon remains necessary.

Because a thermostat is a connected device, security testing belongs in the toolchain from the start, with roughly 75 billion connected embedded devices expected online by 2025 and over 2,000 embedded-specific vulnerabilities already catalogued in the National Vulnerability Database.

Concretely, static firmware analysis with open tools like Binwalk and Firmwalker can extract filesystems and hunt for hardcoded credentials, while dynamic analysis boots the same image inside QEMU for probing with tools like Nmap, closing the loop between emulation-based testing and security posture.

Baseline defenses worth budgeting for include secure boot verification, encrypted and authenticated firmware updates, and tamper-detection logic, since an unauthenticated update path is one of the most common ways connected products get compromised.

Put together, a practical path is to prototype control logic in QEMU or Verilator simulation, settle on a RISC-V or Cortex-M core running FreeRTOS or Zephyr for the control loop, add Buildroot-built Linux only if networking is required, and validate the final image with open-source static and dynamic security tooling before flashing real hardware.
